Article Title: A Utah couple wanted a place to scuba without travelling, so they built a $2 million, 360,000-gallon backyard pool with a 90-foot mountain, five waterfalls, a 300-foot lazy river and a 26-foot-deep di
Article Text:
Photo: Crazy World

A 90-foot mountain in the backyard

A tunnel that lets the owners practise scuba diving

Photo: Crazy World

A kitchen, bridges and hidden spaces

A $2 million project featured on television

A Utah couple wanted a place where they could practise scuba diving without travelling to the ocean. Their solution was to build a $2 million backyard swimming pool with 360,000 gallons of water, a 90-foot man-made mountain, five waterfalls and an underwater tunnel that takes divers down to a depth of 26 feet. Called “The Mountain”, the pool was built at a home in Springville, Utah. It stretches 140 feet long and 60 feet wide, and includes a 300-foot lazy river, a hidden grotto, winding pathways and a water slide concealed inside the mountain.As reported by FOX 13 News, the unusual pool was featured on Animal Planet’s television programme ‘The Pool Master,’ hosted by pool designer Anthony Archer-Wills. The project was designed for a homeowner who loved mountains and scuba diving, the broadcaster reported.The pool’s main feature is a 90-foot artificial mountain designed to resemble the natural landscape around the property. It includes five waterfalls, several hidden pathways and two bridges that wind towards the top. Archer-Wills described the structure as one that “emulates the natural surroundings perfectly”, according to FOX 13 News. The mountain is not just decorative. A hidden water slide runs for 60 feet through the structure before dropping into the pool below.There is also a secluded grotto tucked behind the waterfalls, giving swimmers another place to explore. The pool’s design combines these features with a 300-foot lazy river, allowing the owners to swim, float and explore different parts of the property without leaving home.Scuba diving was one of the main reasons the couple commissioned the pool. Utah is far from the ocean, so having a deep-water area at home offered them a place to practise. According to FOX 13 News, a concealed entrance inside the mountain leads to a tunnel measuring 54 feet long and five feet wide. The tunnel reaches a depth of 26 feet and connects to the main pool. The underwater section is intended for scuba-certified divers. It allows them to put on diving equipment and practise underwater skills without travelling to a coastal diving location. As reported by Scuba Diving magazine, the $2 million project included the 54-foot tunnel, five waterfalls, the lazy river and a hidden 60-foot slide in the year 2014.The pool also has facilities for spending time outdoors beyond swimming and diving. According to FOX 13 News, the mountain houses a full kitchen with granite countertops, stainless-steel cabinets, a refrigerator and an eight-burner grill. The bridges and paths offer access to the upper sections of the structure, while the hidden grotto and winding passages give the mountain several enclosed spaces to explore. The combination of water features, diving facilities and kitchen space makes the backyard pool more elaborate than a conventional residential swimming pool.The project came to wider attention when it appeared on ‘The Pool Master,’ a programme that follows pool designer Anthony Archer-Wills as he transforms residential outdoor spaces. The pool cost approximately $2 million to build. In its 2015 report, Scuba Diving magazine highlighted the project as an example of how a private swimming pool could be designed around a specific hobby. For the Utah homeowners, the central purpose was practical as well as recreational: they wanted somewhere to practise scuba diving close to home. The result was a 360,000-gallon pool built around an artificial mountain, with five waterfalls, a lazy river, a hidden slide and a 26-foot-deep underwater tunnel.
Article Summary: A Utah couple wanted a place where they could practise scuba diving without travelling to the ocean. Their solution was to build a $2 million backyard pool with 360,000 gallons of water, a 90-foot man-made mountain, five waterfalls and an underwater tunnel. Called ‘The Mountain’, the pool was built at a home in Springville, Utah. It stretches 140 feet long and 60 feet wide, and includes a 300-foot lazy river, a hidden grotto, winding pathways and a water slide concealed inside the mountain.

Article Title: Google’s Android earthquake alerts expand to 200+ regions with more info; Sundar Pichai explains how it helped in Venezuela
Article Text:
New details added to earthquake alerts

Designed to provide precious seconds of warning

Google has announced a major expansion of its Android Earthquake Alerts System, extending the feature from 98 countries and regions to more than 200 while introducing additional information in earthquake warnings to help users respond more effectively during emergencies. The company also added that the system has managed to deliver more than one billion earthquake alerts since its launch in 2021, making it what Google describes as the world’s largest mobile-based earthquake detection network. The expanded coverage will bring alerts to more locations including Panama and Guatemala, among others.The announcement was highlighted by Google CEO Sundar Pichai, who said the technology has already aided people during critical moments. In a post on X, Pichai noted that the system has sent over one billion alerts since 2021 and is now expanding from 98 to nearly 200 countries and regions. He also pointed to this year's earthquakes in Venezuela, saying millions of people outside the epicentre received alerts and were able to take cover before the shaking began. “Since launching in 2021, our Android Earthquake Alerts System has sent 1B+ alerts. Now we’re expanding the system from 98 to nearly 200 countries and regions.Proud how this technology can help in moments that really matter. As one example, when the devastating earthquakes hit Venezuela this year, millions of people outside the epicenter got alerts and could take cover before the shaking began,” wrote Pichai in a post.Alongside the geographic expansion, Google is enhancing its "Be Ready" earthquake alert with more contextual information. In the coming months, users will see a map showing the radius of detected shaking, the estimated earthquake magnitude, recommended actions, and a button to access more information as details become available.Android users in supported regions may receive one of three alert types depending on the expected intensity of shaking. The "Be Aware" alert is designed for estimated light shaking, while "Be Ready" provides advance notice of stronger shaking and encourages users to prepare. The highest-level "Take Action" alert appears full-screen and offers immediate safety guidance for moderate to heavy shaking.Google said even a few seconds of advance notice can be crucial during an earthquake, giving people time to take cover and protect themselves. The Android Earthquake Alerts System uses mobile devices to help detect seismic activity and deliver warnings before strong shaking reaches users.The company said its safety-focused products play an important role during natural disasters, adding that the latest expansion aims to provide more people with potentially life-saving information when they need it most.
Article Summary: Google has announced a major expansion of its Android Earthquake Alerts System, extending the feature from 98 countries and regions to more than 200. The company added that the system has managed to deliver more than one billion earthquake alerts since its launch in 2021. The expanded coverage will bring alerts to more locations including Panama and Guatemala, among others.

Article Title: Meta releases Muse Spark Open AI model with 816 billion parameters; runs on two Apple Mac Studios
Article Text:
Meta releases Muse Spark Open AI model with 816 billion parameters; runs on two Apple Mac Studios

Meta Muse Spark Open: Features and capabilities

How to access Muse Spark Open AI model

Meta has released Muse Spark Open, an open-weight artificial intelligence (AI) model designed for coding, complex reasoning and tasks that require multiple steps. The company says the model can run on a desktop setup using two Apple Mac Studios powered by M5 Ultra chips, making it possible to use an advanced AI model locally rather than relying only on cloud services. As stated by the company in its official announcement, Muse Spark Open has 816 billion total parameters, with 42 billion active parameters, and supports a context window of 1 million tokens. Developers can access the model through several AI platforms or download its weights to customize it for their needs.Meta said Muse Spark Open is designed for long-running tasks, complex software development and agentic AI workflows, in which a model can carry out multiple steps towards a goal.The model is natively multimodal, meaning it can work with different types of information. It has 816 billion total parameters, of which 42 billion are active, and a context window of 1 million tokens. A large context window allows a model to process a substantial amount of information in a single interaction.Meta said it tested the model on tasks involving software development and video editing. In one test, the model was used to make bug fixes and add features to Ice Cubes, an open-source Mastodon client, before building the application.In another, it worked with DaVinci Resolve to review video footage frame by frame, identify suitable moments and crop clips into a vertical format.The company also said the model includes optimised GPU kernels that deliver kernel-level speed improvements of 1.03 to 3.95 times on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. Meta reported a 3% overall speed improvement on AMD MI350.Meta says Muse Spark Open is available through AI inference platforms including Baseten, Fireworks AI, Groq, Modal, Nebius, OpenRouter and Together AI. Developers can download its model weights through Hugging Face, Amazon SageMaker AI, Google Cloud Model Garden and Microsoft Foundry Models. The model supports inference engines such as SGLang, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, Hugging Face Transformers, Apple MLX, llama.cpp and Unsloth. Developers can also customise it using PyTorch.For local use, Meta has optimised Muse Spark Open for Apple's M5 Ultra Mac Studio through the MLX framework. According to the company, two Mac Studios can work together to provide enough unified memory to hold the model.Meta said it has added safety training to the open-weight version and evaluated it under its Superintelligence Scaling Framework. The company said the model met the safety thresholds required for release.The model is being released under the Muse Model License, which allows many developers to use it for free but includes limited commercial terms. Its weights are available through the Muse Spark Open collection on Hugging Face.
Article Summary: Muse Spark Open is designed for coding, complex reasoning and tasks that require multiple steps. The model is natively multimodal, meaning it can work with different types of information. It has 816 billion total parameters, of which 42 billion are active, and a context window of 1 million tokens.

Article Title: Years after telling Meta employees to inflict pain on Apple, Mark Zuckerberg sends 'thanks note' to Apple CEO John Ternus; gets a 'reply'
Article Text:
Apple and Meta are on speaking terms again

Meta's most capable open AI model now runs on Apple's Mac Studio

Apple's privacy push cost Meta billions and sparked years of barbs

A former Apple executive helped bring Meta and Apple back to the table

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has publicly thanked Apple 's new CEO John Ternus , and Ternus has written back. The exchange happened on X on Thursday, when Meta released the weights for Muse Spark Open. That's Meta's new open-weight AI model, and the two companies spent months tuning it to run locally on Apple's Mac Studio desktops. Zuckerberg shared a picture of Meta's AI agent at work on a Mac. He wrote that the model "runs great on new Mac Studios thanks to work with @johnternus and Apple."Ternus took over from Tim Cook last month. He replied "Congrats to the team!" and said Mac Studio "keeps pushing the boundaries of on-device AI." It is a far cry from 2021. That year, Apple's App Tracking Transparency feature hit Facebook's ad business, and Zuckerberg reportedly told employees the company needed to "inflict pain" on Apple.Muse Spark Open is an 816-billion-parameter model built on a mixture-of-experts design. Meta calls it the most capable US-developed open-weight model to date. It is aimed at long coding sessions, multi-step reasoning and video analysis. The model is free to download from platforms like Hugging Face, and its licence allows commercial use with some limits.The setup links two or four Mac Studios running Apple's M5 Ultra chip.Apple's MLX framework splits the model across those machines. Apple has also put out new benchmarks and technical notes on how MLX handles open models of this size. Since everything stays on the desk, Meta does not see the prompts or files developers feed it. "Meta has no control or visibility to any of that," Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang said.It does not come cheap. An M5 Ultra Mac Studio with 256GB of memory costs over Rs 9 lakh at US prices, and the model needs at least two. A 512GB version is due later this month.The bad blood goes back years. In 2018, at the height of the Cambridge Analytica scandal, Cook was asked what he would do in Zuckerberg's shoes. "I wouldn't be in this situation," he said. Zuckerberg called the remark "extremely glib."Then iOS 14.5 arrived in 2021. It made apps ask permission before tracking users across other apps and websites, and most iPhone owners chose not to be tracked. Meta later estimated the change would cut its 2022 revenue by $10 billion. As recently as last year, Zuckerberg told podcaster Joe Rogan that Apple "hasn't invented anything great since the iPhone."The two have not struck a public partnership since 2017, when Apple pulled Facebook's built-in integration from iOS.Wang credits Daniel Gross with getting the two sides to work together. Gross is a former Apple executive who joined Meta's AI push last year. "Most of the animosity predates my tenure at the company," Wang said in an interview. He added that he was "excited for mommy and daddy to be playing nice again."Both sides get something here. Apple gets to show its chips can handle heavy AI work away from Nvidia-powered data centres. Meta gets its model in front of developers who might later pay to scale up. Apple already uses Google's Gemini models in Apple Intelligence, and its relationship with OpenAI has ended up in court.Neither company would say if more is coming. The real test would be Meta's models showing up inside Apple Intelligence. For now, the change is mostly one of tone. Five years after talking about inflicting pain on Apple, Zuckerberg is tagging its CEO by name, and Ternus is replying with exclamation marks.
Article Summary: Meta's most capable open-weight AI model now runs on Apple's Mac Studio. Zuckerberg shared a picture of Meta's AI agent at work on a Mac. He wrote that the model "runs great on new Mac Studios thanks to work with @johnternus and Apple"

Article Title: Can technology prevent the next stampede? Inside the crowd-monitoring tools India needs
Article Text:
Digital ticketing, people counters and entry gates fed with live occupancy data can help organizers prevent a venue from exceeding its safe capacity.

Live alerts can help officials prevent dangerous crowd surges

Digital ticketing, people counters and entry gates fed with live occupancy data can help organizers prevent a venue from exceeding its safe capacity.

Predicting disaster to documenting

Real-time crowd monitoring needs coordinated emergency response systems

AI cameras can detect crowd build-up

Narrow exits, poorly placed barricades and inadequate evacuation plans can worsen stampede risks despite advanced technology.

Crowd safety depends on swift action after alerts

How alerts are only useful

Access clear announcements

Tech can't replace ground level planning

Next step: real-time crowd safety network





NEW DELHI: Nineteen people were killed and 25 injured in the stampede at Kolkata’s Chorbagan Durga Puja pandal on Saturday, bringing crowd management back into focus.Heavy rain was said to have driven visitors toward the entrance, causing a stampede in which people fell over each other. The tragedy raises an important question: can technology identify the warning signs before a crowd turns dangerous?India has invested heavily in CCTV cameras in public places, transport hubs and mass gatherings. But cameras that just record events are of little use in preventing a stampede. Artificial intelligence (AI) can analyze live video feeds, estimate crowd density, track movement and flag sudden surges, so control rooms can identify trouble spots before conditions become critical. The challenge is to turn surveillance into an early warning system that leads to action.Such systems can count people entering and exiting a venue, map congestion at individual gates and identify areas where flow has slowed or reversed.Algorithms can also spot unusual clustering, sudden changes in the direction of crowds and people falling. During the 2025 Maha Kumbh in Prayagraj, an integrated command and control center was deployed to monitor crowd density and movement utilizing inputs from 500 AI-enabled cameras and drones.A monitoring system has to be more than just flashing a warning on a screen. Alerts should be sent to police officers, event organizers and teams managing entry and exit points when density exceeds a pre-set safety threshold.Officials may be able to temporarily stop incoming visitors, create designated dispersal routes, redirect people from choke points or place personnel to relieve pressure. Importantly, thresholds should be based on the layout of the venue and the patterns of movement, not on a single crowd-count figure.Digital ticketing, people counters and entry gates fed with live occupancy data can help organizers prevent a venue from exceeding its safe capacity. Connect public address systems to crowd-control teams so instructions are consistent as conditions change. Heavy rain is said to have contributed to the rush. It could also lead to weather alerts and precautionary measures at Kolkata. These may include temporary entry restrictions, additional personnel deployment, and clear directions for visitors.Even the most sophisticated artificial intelligence can't make up for narrow exits, badly placed barricades or insufficient evacuation plans. Cameras can also fail to capture activity in blind spots and can be affected by rain, poor lighting or dense crowds, which can affect the quality of readings. So every major event needs a physical safety audit, clearly marked emergency routes, trained personnel and medical teams and regular evacuation drills. Technology should reinforce these arrangements, not give a false sense of security.India needs a common operating framework for high-footfall religious gatherings, festivals, railroad stations and public events connecting CCTV analytics, entry counts, weather alerts and emergency response teams.Authorities should also carry out post-event audits to determine if alerts were issued and acted on in a timely manner. As adoption grows, privacy protections and independent verification of automated systems will be critical. The real test is not how many cameras a venue installs but whether its safety system is able to detect danger early enough to move people out of harm’s way.
Article Summary: Digital ticketing, people counters and entry gates fed with live occupancy data can help organizers prevent a venue from exceeding its safe capacity. Artificial intelligence (AI) can analyze live video feeds, estimate crowd density, track movement and flag sudden surges. Even the most sophisticated artificial intelligence can't make up for narrow exits, badly placed barricades or insufficient evacuation plans.

Article Title: An 18-year-old built an AI traffic system that changes pedestrian signals based on how safe people feel crossing a road
Article Text:
Phillips Academy student Jay Jung of Massachusetts. Image Credit: Impacto Positivo

How does the 18-year-old's AI traffic system make pedestrian crossings safer

Image Credit: Jay Jing/NiceNews

The idea began with a problem involving his grandparents

SmartBlink adjusts crossing time for speed of walking

The student received international recognition for his invention

An 18-year-old student has developed an AI-powered traffic system designed to make road crossings safer for people who need more time to reach the other side. The system is called SmartBlink and instead of a set time for crossing, it changes the pedestrian light timings based on how fast people cross the road. The invention, developed by Phillips Academy student Jay Jung of Massachusetts, aims to make streets more accessible to older adults and others with physical difficulties. His work has also earned recognition at an international science competition.Traditional pedestrian signals give people a limited amount of time to cross a road. While this arrangement may work for many pedestrians, it can leave older adults and people with mobility difficulties struggling to reach the pavement before the signal changes.For Jung, this was not simply a technical problem but something he had noticed during everyday life. His experience walking with his grandparents led him to explore how traffic signals might better serve people moving at various speeds, NiceNews reported.His invention, SmartBlink, uses AI to monitor pedestrian movement and adjust crossing times accordingly. Instead of expecting everyone to cross at the same pace, the system takes account of how long the slower-moving pedestrian may need.The project reflects a different approach to road safety, placing greater emphasis on the people using a crossing instead of treating every pedestrian as though they have identical physical abilities.Jung grew up with his grandparents in South Korea. During his childhood, he noticed that they sometimes struggled to cross streets in Seoul before pedestrian signals changed.Walking with his grandparents to places such as the local grocery shop and park helped him recognise the limitations of conventional crossing signals. The time allowed to cross did not always match the pace at which they could comfortably walk.That experience stayed with him, and eventually influenced how he approached technology. He began to wonder if a more responsive system might be a practical solution. His project exemplifies how a simple observation can lead to an idea that goes beyond the original problem.The main advantage of SmartBlink is its capacity to estimate the time a pedestrian needs to cross the road. Instead of following an unchanging schedule, the system can adapt the crossing period to the person's observed movement.If a pedestrian signal normally provides 20 seconds to cross, but the system estimates that a person needs 34 seconds, it can add another 14 seconds to the crossing period.This adjustment is intended to reduce the pressure pedestrians may feel when trying to reach the other side before the light changes. It also recognises that crossing a road can be more challenging for someone who walks slowly or uses a mobility aid.According to NiceNews, SmartBlink can identify pedestrians using wheelchairs, crutches or walking canes. Its algorithm has also been adapted to function under different lighting conditions, supporting its potential use during both daytime and night-time hours.A crossing that works well for one person may not provide enough time for another. SmartBlink seeks to address that difference by adapting the signal to the person crossing.Jung's work received recognition at the 2026 Regeneron International Science and Engineering Fair, an international competition for secondary-school students presenting scientific and engineering projects.According to the Society for Science, Jung won 1st place in the Behavioral and Social Sciences category for SmartBlink. The project was recognised under the title ‘SmartBlink: Real-Time AI-Driven Adaptive Pedestrian Traffic System for Enhancing Perceived Pedestrian Safety and Traffic Efficiency.’The award came with a prize of $6,000. The recognition placed his project among a broad range of student-led research initiatives exploring practical problems through science and technology. In Jung's case, the focus was on making existing urban infrastructure more responsive to the people who depend on it.Despite the award, the system has not yet been installed at pedestrian crossings. Its next stage involves exploring how it could be tested in actual communities and adapted to local conditions.
Article Summary: Jay Jung, 18, of Massachusetts, developed the system called SmartBlink. Instead of a set time for crossing, it changes the pedestrian light timings based on how fast people cross the road. It aims to make streets more accessible to older adults and others with physical difficulties.

Article Title: A Buckinghamshire wildlife garden redesigned around an unheated natural swimming pond that attracts frogs, bats, and dragonflies
Article Text:
Image: Julie Skelton

A wildlife and wellbeing brief, how Rachel Platt connected a Buckinghamshire garden to the countryside

Inside the unheated natural swimming pool, a plant-free swim zone and a planted regeneration zone

Frogs, toads, newts, dragonflies, bats, and birds, all the wildlife that has moved into the garden's ponds

The existing terrace and two ponds were kept for their environmental value (Image: Julie Skelton)

How drainage reshaped the plan and kept old favourites

Edible hedgerow, uncut winter meadow, and autumn colour; planting that completes the wildlife garden

A place where the daily swim could begin at the back door, surrounded by dragonflies and flowering plants, even in winter, was the dream of two owners in south Buckinghamshire, who work in the veterinary sector and wanted a garden connected to the surrounding fields. Garden designer Rachel Platt answered with an unheated natural swimming pool, a sweeping chalk meadow, and an edible hedgerow. The result attracts frogs, bats, dragonflies, and more. Read on to discover how the design works, which plants and features support wildlife, what changed along the way, and how the owners describe their transformed outdoor sanctuary. The garden shows how thoughtful landscaping can combine everyday enjoyment with a thriving habitat, creating a peaceful retreat that evolves with the seasons.According to Homes and Gardens, which featured the project in an article by Rachel Bull, the owners both work in the veterinary sector and dreamed of a garden linked to the rolling fields and hedgerows around them. Their brief asked for a biodiverse landscape that would support wildlife while also providing space to swim, grow food, entertain, and spend more time outdoors. Rachel Platt Garden Design responded with a layout that deliberately changes character as it moves away from the house: stronger geometry near the building gives way to softer curves, a sweeping chalk meadow, and an experimental edible hedgerow toward the fields beyond.Before the redesign, the owners regularly drove elsewhere to swim in rivers and spent relatively little time in their own garden, so the new design was meant to bring that experience home.At the heart of the garden sits an unheated natural swimming pool, created as both a wildlife habitat and a place for the owners to reconnect with nature, Homes and Gardens reports. Designer Rachel Platt developed it in collaboration with Ellicar Natural Pools. The pool is divided into a swim zone, kept clear of plants and wildlife, and a regeneration zone planted with a range of aquatic species that filter the water naturally, a process the article calls hydrobotanical filtration. Around the shoreline, water mint, water forget-me-nots, native flag irises, marsh marigolds, ragged robin, and purple loosestrife add colour, seasonal structure, and fragrance, flowering from March to September and attracting pollinators and moths. Deeper-growing aquatics such as common water plantain and arrowhead offer late summer flowers and seedheads, and give emerging dragonflies stems to climb while they unfurl their wings.The wildlife has arrived in force. Homes and Gardens reports that dragonflies and bats were already drawn to the pool, with planting softening its edges and tying it into the wider ecosystem. The owners told Homes and Gardens that frogs, toads, and newts breed in all the ponds, as do several dragonfly species, and that they have even spotted a water snake. Birds also visit, using a beach area, a feature not found in conventional ponds, to enter the water and bathe safely. The owners described the pond as a total escape through every season, and said the garden has become a haven where they feel miles away from everything. For anyone planning a wildlife garden, the lesson is that a single well-planned water feature can support amphibians, insects, mammals, and birds at the same time.The pool was not always meant to be round. According to Homes and Gardens, the original concept was a formal linear pond positioned to reflect a mature birch tree visible through large French doors off the open-plan kitchen and living space. Existing drainage and a suspected utility service running across the garden forced a rethink, and the design became a circular pool. Sustainability and sentiment guided other decisions too. The existing terrace and two ponds were kept for their environmental value and the wildlife they support, and much of the existing planting was saved or relocated, including the owners' fig tree, lily of the valley, raspberries, and rhubarb. Reusing what already works reduces waste and preserves habitat, while keeping familiar plants gives the new garden a sense of continuity with the owners' past.Beyond the pool, an edible hedge links the garden to the landscape, Homes and Gardens says, combining common hazel, hawthorn, blackberry, black chokeberry, damson, pear, and serviceberry to provide structure, blossom, fruit, and habitat. It leads gradually into the meadow, which the owners deliberately leave uncut over winter so that insects, birds, and small mammals can feed on seeds and find a place to overwinter. Autumn colour was also requested, so ornamental grasses such as Miscanthus 'Beth Chatto' and perennials such as Ceratostigma plumbaginoides and white gaura carry warm tones, while burning bush adds bright red. A kitchen garden, grapevine pergola, firepit, and outdoor shower complete the picture. Summing up the transformation, the owners told Homes and Gardens, "We really have our own little Eden," and called the redesign the best decision they have ever made.
Article Summary: Two owners in Buckinghamshire wanted a garden connected to the surrounding fields. Garden designer Rachel Platt designed an unheated natural swimming pool, a sweeping chalk meadow, and an edible hedgerow. The result attracts frogs, toads, newts, dragonflies, bats, and birds.

Article Title: In a 1986 field test, engineers added tiny vortex generators to turbine blades; annual energy output rose nearly 6% at one test site
Article Text:
AI-generated representative image showing a wind turbine rising above agricultural fields, illustrating efforts to improve wind energy production. Credits - Gemini

Why little fins are good

What the 1986 test revealed

AI-generated representative image showing small vortex generators attached to a wind turbine blade to help control airflow over its surface. Credits - Gemini

Where the profits end up

A wind turbine blade works like an aviation wing. For the blade to provide lift and continue rotating, air must flow smoothly over its curved surface. When that smooth flow separates from the surface, lift decreases, drag increases, and the turbine wastes wind that could have been converted into power. For decades, engineers have struggled with this issue, and one of the least expensive solutions is also one of the smallest. To alter the way air behaves as it passes, tiny fins that are only a small portion of the blade's width can be adhered to the surface in tidy rows. Wind energy has a surprisingly lengthy history with what are known as vortex generators. NASA contractor study dated July 1986 gave some actual data on that history. The paper was written by G. W. Gyatt of the California company AeroVironment and reported on field experiments of vortex generators on a tiny turbine dubbed the Carter Model 25. The fins covered the full blade, and at one test site energy output increased by about 6% annually. That sounds humble. But it was off an inexpensive add-on and was measured on a real machine in actual wind, not on a computer model.A vortex generator is a tiny vane that is angled to the oncoming air.The fin makes a little whirlpool when the wind blows past it. This whirlpool is called a vortex. That swirl draws faster-moving air down into the slow, sticky stuff that's clinging to the blade, and the electrified layer stays around longer before the airflow separates and the blade stalls. Wind engineers borrowed the trick, which was first devised to delay stall on aeroplane wings.There is another reason turbine blades can benefit from vortex generators. Insects, dust and grime collect on the leading edge and roughen the surface, disrupting the smooth flow the blade was supposed to have. The 1986 team went straight to the test and added roughness strips to simulate bug and dirt buildup and checked to see if the fins would mitigate the damage. They did. A dirty leading edge was a performance killer, but the fins more than made up for that. A wonderful bonus for blades that spend years outside.The Carter Model 25 was a tiny machine with a rotor of around 32 ft (9.8 m) in diameter. The engineers tested the fins in three configurations: on the inner half of each blade, on the outer half and over the whole length. The fins were paired, and the vortices were rotated in opposite directions. Each was four times as long as high, and its height was barely half to one percent of the breadth of the blade.The results varied with wind speed. Above about 10 metres per second (22 miles per hour), the fins increased power output by as much as 20%; at lower wind speeds, they caused a performance penalty of less than 4%. That penalty did not necessarily cancel out the gains over an entire year, because annual energy production reflects performance across the site's full range of wind conditions. Fins on the outer half of the blade performed better than those on the inner half. The full-span configuration increased annual energy output by nearly 6% at a site with an average wind speed of 16 miles per hour (about 7.2 metres per second).There were other ways to change the power curve. The 1986 team noted that increasing the blade pitch angle could produce a similar effect. Vortex generators had another advantage: they reduced performance losses caused by dirt and insects accumulating along the blade's leading edge. Their use on wind turbines dated to 1983, when they were tested on the much larger Boeing MOD-2 machine, increasing annual energy production by 11% to 15%. Results from that earlier test were subsequently scaled to develop the configuration used on the Carter Model 25, as a 1996 NREL review explains.The aerodynamics of the MOD 2 blades were less than optimal; therefore, there remained space for improvement. Other turbine designs may gain less from vortex generators, depending on their blade geometry and sensitivity to surface roughness. A separate NREL-funded project in the mid-1990s tested vortex generators on the AWT-26, a two-bladed turbine with a 26.2-metre rotor. Although the fins increased power output at moderate wind speeds, drag reduced output at lower speeds enough to produce a net decline in annual energy at sites with average wind speeds up to 8.5 metres per second (about 19 miles per hour), according to NREL's report.Newer evidence, with careful placement of the fins, looks more promising. In a 2020 study in the journal Wind Energy, which can be seen on the research portal of DTU , the Technical University of Denmark, fins were evaluated on megawatt-scale turbines affected by surface roughness. Over 27 months, six turbines were involved, three of which had fins, and each had a neighbour as a reference. All three installed turbines produced more energy afterwards, with the average gain being 3.3% compared to the 2.8% projected by the authors' model.The researchers also warned that vortex generators placed in the wrong part of a blade, or designed too large or too far out, can reduce annual energy production. Engineering modelling is therefore necessary before the devices are installed on a specific turbine, because their effects depend on blade design, surface condition and the local wind regime. Vortex generators can improve airflow over turbine blades, but their effectiveness depends on the blade design, surface condition and local wind regime. The Carter Model 25 test and later trials show that gains at some wind speeds can be offset by added drag at others. Careful modelling and site-specific testing are therefore essential before fitting the devices to an existing turbine.
Article Summary: Vortex generators are a tiny vane that is angled to the oncoming air. The fin makes a whirlpool when the wind blows past it. This swirl draws faster-moving air down into the slow, sticky stuff that's clinging to the blade. The electrified layer stays around longer before the airflow separates and the blade stalls.

Article Title: In 2010, artists began turning a vacant Houston lot into a park using broken dishes, bottle caps, shells, keys and discarded tiles; 16 years later, more than 300 artists have filled it with a 400-foot
Article Text:
Smither Park transforms discarded materials into public art, reflecting Houston’s diverse communities, creative spirit and ever-evolving identity through colour and imagination.

From vacant lot to visual wonder

A wall made of memories

Whimsy at every turn

Art without a price tag

A portrait of Houston

What began as an abandoned patch of land in southeast Houston has slowly transformed into something far more magical: a public park assembled from the fragments of everyday life. Broken crockery, discarded tiles, shells, bottle caps, keys and scraps of found objects have found new purpose here, brought together by hundreds of artists into a sprawling celebration of colour, memory and imagination.Sixteen years after work began, Smither Park has become a living example of what can happen when discarded materials are given another chance, states an October 2016 report by the Houston Chronicle.According to the online report, before artists arrived, the half-acre site on Munger Street was little more than an eyesore. The land, already owned by the Orange Show Center for Visionary Art, was chosen for a new park dedicated to the memory of John Smither, a collector and supporter of outsider art.His wife, Stephanie Smither, a longtime Orange Show board member, wanted the space to honour his legacy. The project found an ideal creative partner in builder and artist Dan Phillips, whose work frequently incorporates reclaimed and discarded materials, adds the report.Construction began in 2010, with the foundations of what would become the park's signature feature: a 400-foot mosaic memory wall.As per the report, the wall is less a conventional piece of public art than a giant collage assembled from thousands of fragments. Bathroom tiles sit alongside nail polish bottles, shells, clay figures, broken dishes and other salvaged objects.Across its length, the colourful surface forms animals, abstract patterns and playful figures. More than 300 artists have contributed to the project over the years, turning individual pieces of material into a collective artwork.The result feels deliberately eclectic and nothing appears too precious or perfectly matched. Instead, the charm comes from the unexpected combinations and the sense that almost anything can become part of the composition.According to the report, the mosaic wall is only the beginning. Over the years, the park has grown to include a pavilion decorated with recycled glass bottles, a fish-themed band shell, a swing set, a meditation garden and a marble tower.The tower is among the park's more interactive attractions, designed around the simple pleasure of watching a marble travel through an elaborate sequence of cups, saucers, roasting pans and fan blades. Its playful mechanics fit naturally into a space where art is meant to be touched, explored and experienced rather than simply observed.The park's various structures each have their own visual language, yet the use of recycled and donated materials ties everything together.The report claims that the project was completed for around $1.2 million, largely through private donations. Many of the artists contributed their time without payment, while much of the material was donated, recycled or rescued from being discarded. That approach is central to Smither Park's character. Its raw materials are not hidden behind polished finishes. Their previous lives remain visible, giving the work an unusual sense of history.Even after the park's formal opening, the creative process has continued. Artists still visit the materials warehouse, sorting through boxes of fragments in search of something that might complete their next idea.More than a collection of colourful objects, Smither Park has become a portrait of its city and its people. Its mixture of cultures, materials, ideas and artistic styles reflects a place that is constantly being rebuilt and reimagined.The park's greatest achievement may be the way it turns the overlooked into the unforgettable. A broken dish becomes part of a wall; a discarded bottle becomes a detail in a pavilion; an empty lot becomes a gathering place.Images Courtesy: Houston Chronicle
Article Summary: Smither Park is a public park in southeast Houston, Texas, dedicated to the memory of John Smither, a collector and supporter of outsider art. More than 300 artists have contributed to the project over the years, turning individual pieces of material into a collective artwork. The project was completed for around $1.2 million, largely through private donations.

Article Title: At Louisiana’s Fort Polk, researchers spread pulverized classified paper on damaged Army land; native plant cover was 48% higher at one soil site and 42% higher at another
Article Text:
Representative AI image of a tractor-mounted spreader distributing pulverised paper. (Image Credits: ChatGPT)

Soil and Tillage Research

How researchers tested the paper amendment

Representative image of a military training ground. (Image Credits: Pexels)

Different soil conditions produced different results

Researchers at Fort Polk, Louisiana, investigated whether pulverised classified paper waste could help restore military training land. Military training grounds can experience soil disturbance from movement of vehicles and soldiers across the land, making vegetation establishment more difficult. The US Agricultural Research Service (ARS) reported that native plant cover was 45% higher on plots receiving the recommended paper treatment compared to control plots. The experiment examined whether shredded paper could serve as a soil amendment while providing an alternative use for waste otherwise sent to landfill. The findings were published in 2019 in, wherein researchers recommended applying pulverised paper at 35.9 metric tonnes per hectare.The field experiment began in April 2015, when researchers spread pulverised paper obtained from document-shredding facilities across experimental plots and incorporated it into the upper 15 centimetres of soil. They then planted four native warm-season grasses: big bluestem, Indiangrass, little bluestem and switchgrass.The experiment used two soil types; the first was an Alfisol, taken from more fertile soil conditions at one site, while the second was an Ultisol, which had lower fertility.Different quantities of paper were then applied at each location, and the results were compared to untreated control plots and plots that were treated with conventional soil.The rates differed because the researchers encountered difficulties incorporating the highest application levels into the Alfisol soil. The Ultisol plots received rates of 17.9, 35.9, 53.8 and 71.7 metric tonnes per hectare, and the rates at the Alfisol site were 9.0, 17.9, 26.9 and 35.9 metric tonnes per hectare. Consequently, 71.7 metric tonnes per hectare was the highest rate tested at the Ultisol site.The conventional treatment consisted of lime, applied at 2,240 kilograms per hectare, and nitrogen fertiliser at 56 kilograms of nitrogen per hectare. The control plots received neither amendment nor fertiliser, although they were prepared and seeded in the same way as the other plots.The scientific paper provides the site-specific figures behind the findings, and at the Alfisol site, native plant cover at 35.9 metric tonnes per hectare was 48% higher than the control and 62% higher than the conventional treatment. Conversely, at the Ultisol site, native plant cover at 71.7 metric tonnes per hectare, the highest rate tested there, was 42% higher than the control and 17% higher than the conventional treatment.In terms of plant cover and plant biomass, different results were also produced. At the Ultisol site, native plant biomass at 71.7 metric tonnes per hectare was 71% lower than the control, while the conventional treatment produced 355% more. At the Alfisol site, native plant biomass at 35.9 metric tonnes per hectare was 90% higher than the control and 96% higher than the conventional treatment. These measurements indicate that greater plant cover did not necessarily mean greater plant biomass across both sites.The researchers linked the contrasting responses to differences in nutrient availability. The Ultisol site showed improvements in certain physical and chemical soil properties, but its low fertility meant that nitrogen immobilisation could constrain grass growth. At the more fertile Alfisol site, the carbon-rich paper tied up nitrogen, which helped reduce competition from weeds and invasive plants and favoured the planted native grasses. ARS also reported estimated savings of about $11,600 per hectare and annual savings of around $20,000 per military facility, alongside a potential diversion of about 64 metric tonnes of paper from landfill. Subsequently, the Corps of Engineers produced a user guide based on the research to help military facilities consider the approach to land rehabilitation.
Article Summary: Researchers at Fort Polk, Louisiana, investigated whether pulverised classified paper waste could help restore military training land. Military training grounds can experience soil disturbance from movement of vehicles and soldiers across the land. The US Agricultural Research Service reported that native plant cover was 45% higher on plots receiving the recommended paper treatment.

Article Title: Nominee vs legal heir: What is the difference and who has claim on assets? All you need to know
Article Text:

Who is a Nominee?



Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.

How Jeevan Pramaan simplifies pensioner verification



Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.
Article Summary: A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.

CIBIL credit score : Understanding your creditworthiness is pivotal in today's financial landscape, especially when seeking loans or credit cards. Your credit history influences your CIBIL score , which is calculated using a special method.Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.1. Go to the official CIBIL website and click on 'Personal CIBIL score,' then 'Get Your Free CIBIL score.' Follow the link provided and fill in all the required details.2. If you don’t have a PAN Card, you can use an alternative identification such as Passport, Voter ID, Driver’s License, or Ration Card. Enter the number of the chosen ID.3. Provide your date of birth, PIN code, and select your state. Finally, enter your mobile number and click on ‘Accept and Continue’.4. Choose whether you want to link the device with your account. Select 'Yes' or 'No' based on your preference.6. Article Title: More adult nappies, more pet prams? What Japan and Korea’s numbers really say
Article Text:
Japan’s adult nappy production and South Korea’s pet-stroller sales reveal shifting demographics (AI-generated image)

When adult nappies overtook baby nappies

illustration

Pet strollers sell more than baby strollers

Two small objects offer a striking glimpse of demographic change in Japan and South Korea: a nappy and a pram. But the numbers behind them answer different questions.In Japan, more than 10 billion adult incontinence products were produced in 2025, against just over 7.1 billion baby nappies. That is a comparison by number of pieces. The adult count includes pads and liners as well as nappies and pants. It measures production, which is not necessarily the same as the number bought or used in Japan.South Korea’s 2025 finding looks similar at first: 61,418 tonnes of adult products supplied, compared with 54,001 tonnes of child products. The adult category overtook the child category by weight in 2024 and stayed ahead in 2025. But a heavier pile need not contain more nappies. Both Korean categories also include hygiene underpads.How different might the count be? One Japanese study calculated an average weight of 62.4g for an adult nappy and 32.1g for a baby nappy. Applying those weights to Korea’s supply gives the following, not an estimate of actual Korean sales:Those weights come from Japan and do not account for the mix of products in Korea’s supply.They cannot establish Korea’s actual piece count. They do show why the distinction matters: adult supply weighs about 14% more, yet could comprise fewer individual products. For adult products to lead by number, their average weight would have to be less than about 14% greater than the child average.The pram finding has a different boundary. On Gmarket, a South Korean online shopping marketplace, pet strollers accounted for 58% of pet and baby stroller sales by number through September 2024; baby strollers accounted for 42%. The result describes sales on Gmarket. It does not tell us which type sold more across every shop in South Korea, or how many homes have pets and children.The three figures are revealing when read precisely: Japan’s adult products lead by pieces produced; Korea’s adult products lead by weight supplied; and pet strollers led on Gmarket. Each captures part of a changing market. The unit and the source determine exactly what we can say about it.
Article Summary: In Japan, more than 10 billion adult incontinence products were produced in 2025, against just over 7.1 billion baby nappies. The adult category overtook the child category by weight in 2024 and stayed ahead in 2025. On Gmarket, a South Korean online shopping marketplace, pet strollers accounted for 58% of pet and baby stroller sales.

Article Title: Researchers equip giant cockroaches with medical backpacks, fitted with cameras and syringes, the cyborgs search trapped survivors to deliver life-saving aid in disasters
Article Text:
Image credit: X (Twitter)

How these cyborg cockroaches work

What the tests reveal about the technology

How search and rescue teams could use them

Giant cockroaches could help rescue survivors after disasters. Researchers in Australia are developing cyborg-like insects equipped with miniature backpacks containing cameras, electronics and syringe systems designed to deliver emergency medication. The technology aims to help search-and-rescue teams locate injured people trapped beneath rubble and provide medical assistance when direct access is difficult.Called “paraborgs,” these modified insects combine their natural ability to navigate confined spaces with remotely controlled equipment. Scientists are testing whether the cockroaches can carry medical supplies into hazardous areas, identify potential victims through camera feeds and deliver drugs to targets. The approach could eventually support emergency responders dealing with collapsed buildings, earthquakes and other disasters where time and access are critical.According to a BGR report, the project involves researchers associated with the University of Queensland and the University of New South Wales. By combining insect movement with miniature electronic systems, the team aims to reach places conventional rescue equipment may struggle to access.The project uses the giant burrowing cockroach, scientifically known as Macropanesthia rhinoceros, a large cockroach species native to Australia. Its size makes it suitable for carrying a small electronic backpack containing a camera, control equipment and a syringe-based delivery mechanism.Unlike conventional robotic devices, these insects retain their natural ability to move through tight spaces. Researchers use implanted electrodes to stimulate the cockroaches' nervous systems, letting operators remotely control their direction. This could help guide them through gaps in collapsed structures and other areas human rescuers cannot easily enter.The cameras mounted on their backs provide a view of the surrounding environment. Rescue teams could use these images to assess obstacles, identify accessible routes and look for people who may be trapped nearby.The medical delivery system is another part of the design. Researchers have developed a mechanism that can fire a small syringe, described as functioning like a dart gun, towards a target. The aim is to deliver medication when a person needs urgent treatment and a medical professional cannot reach them immediately.Potential applications include delivering drugs to people experiencing certain emergencies, such as snakebite or severe allergic reactions. However, the technology remains experimental, and using it in real disaster rescue operations would require further testing.Early testing has examined whether the cockroaches can reach designated checkpoints and successfully deliver medication using the syringe mechanism.According to the reported results, the insects reached the checkpoints with a 100% success rate. The syringe system recorded a 72% success rate when delivering medication to targets. When the syringe was fired from within six inches of a target, the success rate increased to 95%.These results indicate that the insects can navigate designated routes under test conditions, while the distance between the syringe and its target remains an important factor in delivery accuracy.The findings also highlight the distinction between successfully guiding an insect to a location and delivering medicine accurately. In a real emergency, researchers would need to account for uneven terrain, limited visibility, unpredictable movement, and the injured person's condition.Further development would also be necessary to establish how the equipment performs in different environments and whether the system can deliver medication safely and consistently.Search and rescue operations often involve locating people in unstable buildings, collapsed structures and debris-filled areas. Sending rescuers into these environments can be difficult because of restricted access, falling material and the possibility of further structural collapse.Small insects equipped with cameras could provide another way to inspect such locations before a human rescuer enters. Their ability to move through narrow gaps could help teams gather information about spaces that are difficult to examine using larger equipment.Time is another consideration. Finding an injured person quickly can affect the treatment they receive, especially when the emergency involves a condition that requires prompt medical attention. Camera-equipped cockroaches could help rescuers assess a location and identify a possible route towards someone who needs assistance.The technology may also help reduce the physical demands placed on rescue workers. Rather than manually clearing every accessible section of debris, teams could first use the insects to inspect selected areas and determine where further intervention is needed.However, the system would not replace conventional rescue personnel or medical treatment. Its effectiveness would depend on camera visibility, remote control, access to the target, and the ability to safely deliver the appropriate medication.For now, the research demonstrates a potential application of biohybrid technology, which combines living organisms with electronic systems. If further testing establishes its reliability and safety, these cyborg cockroaches could become an additional tool for locating and assisting disaster survivors in places where conventional rescue equipment has limited access.
Article Summary: Researchers in Australia are developing cyborg-like insects equipped with miniature backpacks containing cameras, electronics and syringe systems. The technology aims to help search-and-rescue teams locate injured people trapped beneath rubble and provide medical assistance when direct access is difficult. Scientists are testing whether the cockroaches can carry medical supplies into hazardous areas.

Before Wang could reply, Zuckerberg opened with a lighthearted quip, joking, “I think I can leave now.” Wang quickly followed up with his perspective on their working relationship over the past year.Wang noted that while he does not have an extensive set of comparisons, observing Zuckerberg's management style firsthand revealed unique traits that stand out even within elite tech founder circles:“One of the very cool things about working with Mark over the past year has just been watching the true degree of his boldness,” Wang explained, adding, “Once he internalises certain beliefs, like the speed and magnitude of willing to change prior actions and pivot towards the worldview that is consistent with those beliefs, I think these are pretty unusual traits, generally speaking, even among this base of founders. Very Bayesian.”The analytical praise drew a warm, humorous reaction from Zuckerberg.“Very Bayesian. I've never gotten such a nice compliment,” Zuckerberg responded.A person who follows the Bayesian method relies on statistical inference, using Bayes' theorem to update the probability of a hypothesis as new data or evidence becomes available.Expanding on his observations, Wang admitted that Zuckerberg's appetite for sweeping strategic gambles initially took him by surprise before earning his deep respect.“No, but then I think also just the degree of boldness. It was actually quite puzzling to me at first, the degree to which you were willing to make these massive bets. That is quite a notable trait and something I really admire,” Wang continued.Zuckerberg concluded the exchange with appreciation for the assessment, replying: “I'm so flattered.”

Article Title: Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang reveals the man who made the 'impossible' possible between Apple and Meta
Article Text:
Tim Cook-Mark Zuckerberg once clashed over privacy

Meta's most capable open AI model now runs on Apple's Mac Studio

Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang has revealed that former Apple executive Daniel Gross played a key role in bringing the iPhone-maker and Meta together for an AI collaboration. After years of disagreements, the two companies are now working together to run Meta's new Muse Spark Open AI model on Apple's high-end Mac Studio computers. Their collaboration allows Muse Spark Open, which has 816 billion parameters, to run across two or four connected Mac Studios powered by Apple's M5 Ultra chips, using Apple's MLX framework. Alexandr Wang told Axios that Gross, who now works at Meta, helped the two sides work together. Wang revealed that the two companies had been working together for several months.“I think he played a really big role in kind of getting the two companies to work nicely together,” Alexandr Wang told the publication. “We're excited for mommy and daddy to be playing nice again,” he said.The rivalry between Apple and Meta (then Facebook) dates back to 2018 during the Facebook's Cambridge Analytica scandal. The then Apple CEO Tim Cook was asked what he would do if he were Mark Zuckerberg. Tim Cook then replied saying “I wouldn't be in this situation”.Later, Mark Zuckerberg called Cook's comments "extremely glib.” Again in 2021, when Apple introduced new privacy protections, Zuckerberg told employees that Facebook needed to "inflict pain" on Apple over the dispute, per a report by the Wall Street Journal then.Muse Spark Open is an 816-billion-parameter model built on a mixture-of-experts design. Meta calls it the most capable US-developed open-weight model to date. It is aimed at long coding sessions, multi-step reasoning and video analysis. The model is free to download from platforms like Hugging Face, and its licence allows commercial use with some limits.The setup links two or four Mac Studios running Apple's M5 Ultra chip. Apple's MLX framework splits the model across those machines. Apple has also put out new benchmarks and technical notes on how MLX handles open models of this size. Since everything stays on the desk, Meta does not see the prompts or files developers feed it. "Meta has no control or visibility to any of that," Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang said.It does not come cheap. An M5 Ultra Mac Studio with 256GB of memory costs over Rs 9 lakh at US prices, and the model needs at least two. A 512GB version is due later this month.

Former Apple executive Daniel Gross played a key role in bringing the two companies together for an AI collaboration. The rivalry between Apple and Meta dates back to 2018 during the Facebook's Cambridge Analytica scandal.

Article Title: Google CEO Sundar Pichai, 'Godfather of AI' Yann LeCun reply to Elon Musk post that says ‘future has flying cars’
Article Text:
Tesla roadster demo

Yann LeCun breaks down the physics: ‘Just compressed air’

Even assuming that 50% of the mass of the car is the compressed air, that gives you less than 10s of useful thrust (with thrust-to-weight ratio larger than 1.0).

Probably more like 5 seconds, actually.

So the car must be an empty, lightweight shell containing big compressed air tanks.

Cute demo, but totally impractical.

But of course, you knew that.

Compressed air vs. rocket propulsion

Hydrogen peroxide rockets (like the individual jetpacks of the 1970s) have a specific impulse of 150s, about 3x compressed air, without the annoying exponentially decreasing maximum thrust of compressed air jets.

I originally guessed the car might have used hydrogen peroxide jets because of all the steam. But that's just condensation caused rapid depressurization

Elon Musk set social media abuzz after sharing dramatic footage of a thruster-equipped Tesla Roadster lifting off the ground, somersaulting mid-air and then landing perfectly on ground. The Tesla CEO declared that the “future does have flying cars”. The post triggered massive online engagement, drawing playful reactions from tech peers, including Google CEO Sundar Pichai. However, it also drew technical skepticism from former Meta Chief AI Scientist Yann LeCun, who labeled the stunt a “cute demo, but totally impractical.”As per the video, as the vehicle lifts off, it spews thick plumes of smoke, ‘flies’ over stationary Tesla vehicles, including a Tesla Semi and tumbles as dense vapor blankets the surrounding tarmac. Pichai quipped: “The FSD version of this will be something:) congrats!”Musk responded warmly to the exchange, writing: “Thanks ❤️🚀 It’s such an honor working with incredible engineers.”While the demonstration delighted fans, LeCun took to social media to analyse the underlying mechanics, questioning the vehicle’s real-world feasibility. Initially wondering whether the system ran on hydrogen peroxide rocket propellant, LeCun concluded the thrusters were simply powered by cold gas: “Okay, so it's just compressed air. Easier. But crappy specific impulse (less than 50 seconds).”LeCun argued that the physics behind compressed gas severely restrict flight duration and payload capacity:Drawing comparisons to older aerospace experiments, LeCun pointed out that 1970s-era individual jetpacks relied on hydrogen peroxide rockets, which deliver a specific impulse of roughly 150 seconds.
Article Summary: Elon Musk posted video of himself flying a Tesla Roadster in the air. The stunt drew the attention of tech peers, including Google CEO Sundar Pichai.
